A 10-year-old girl presented with a 1-year history of a rapidly enlarging left breast mass. There was no history of pain, trauma, fever, anorexia, or weight loss. She was premenarcheal, and there was no significant family history. On examination, the left breast had a 20 cm × 20 cm well-circumscribed, firm, non-tender, mobile lump; the right breast was normal. The mass was not fixed to skin or underlying muscle. The overlying skin was tense and shiny with prominent superficial veins. There was no nipple discharge and no axillary lymphadenopathy. Routine hematological and biochemical tests, including ESR, were within normal limits. A chest radiograph was normal. Ultrasonography of the left breast revealed a heterogeneous parenchymal pattern suggestive of fibroadenoma. Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the lump showed pathology suggesting fibroadenoma.

A 20-month-old girl was evaluated for congenital soft-tissue masses and cutaneous vascular lesions. Since birth, she had multiple soft masses on the anterior upper chest, abdomen, and right arm. A large port-wine–colored capillary malformation partially involved her trunk. Examination of the extremities showed hypertrophy of the left thigh, overgrowth of both feet, and syndactyly of the second and third toes on the right. Dilated, tortuous veins were noted over the chest and left leg. She had no facial dysmorphism, no cardiac murmur, no organomegaly, full muscle strength, intact reflexes, and normal developmental milestones and growth parameters.

She was born by cesarean delivery to a nonconsanguineous couple; the pregnancy was notable for fetal malformations. Two older siblings were healthy. Skeletal survey demonstrated fused toes (right second and third, left fourth and fifth) with soft-tissue hypertrophy of the involved digits. 

MRI of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed extensive cystic, septated, high–T2-signal masses consistent with lymphangiomas in the right upper limb, upper chest, upper left lower limb, left pelvis, and retroperitoneum. The liver, kidneys, and pancreas appeared normal, aside from a 12.3-mm hemangioma in the pancreas and a 12-mm hemangioma in the spleen.

clinical_record:
A 54-year-old fisherman with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department after a rapid ascent from a 50 m sea‐depth saturation dive. He complained of dyspnea, lethargy, severe generalized arthralgia, and mild confusion. He was alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. Physical examination showed bilateral joint pain worsened by movement without erythema or swelling; neurological, chest, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Vital signs were blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 95 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, and temperature 36.6 °C. The Wells pulmonary embolism score was 3.

High‐flow oxygen was started. An electrocardiogram was normal. Posterior–anterior chest radiography showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 13 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 73 mg/L, and otherwise normal hemoglobin, platelets, glucose, ESR, creatinine, urea, potassium, sodium, and D-dimer. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated metabolic acidosis with pH 7.32, PCO2 28 mm Hg, HCO3– 15 mmol/L, and PO2 63 mm Hg. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal biventricular size and function and no valvular disease; however, spontaneous echo contrast consistent with microbubbles was seen in the right heart chambers. A Valsalva maneuver–enhanced color‐flow Doppler study showed no evidence of a patent foramen ovale.
